newsitem.title: USA: Koop, Kessler urge Congress to start over on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Koop, Kessler urge Congress to start over on tobacco.

text.p: Leading tobacco critics C. Everett Koop and David Kessler urged lawmakers Tuesday to start afresh in crafting a national tobacco control policy instead of just tinkering with what they called a "flawed" settlement negotiated by the industry and state officials.

Koop, a former U.S. Surgeon General, and Kessler, the former head of the Food and Drug Administration, made their strongest case yet against the proposed settlement before the Senate Commerce Committee.
They said they had come to believe that the deal would leave the cigarette industry "booming and profitable" and do little to combat smoking, the leading preventable cause of death in America.
"The settlement gives the industry practically everythign it wants but shortchanges the public health," said Koop.

Under the complex settlement, tobacco companies would pay $368.5 billion over 25 years, partly for anti-smoking programmes, and make certain marketing concessions. In exchange they would get immunity from certain types of future lawsuits.
Kessler said that would work out to the equivalent of about 62 cents a pack, with the cost passed on to the smoker.
Koop and Kessler said that if making marginal improvements in the pact was the best Congress could do, "Do it."
"But the American people want more and history will not look kindly at your timidness," they added.

Koop and Kessler instead prescribed a simpler six-step programme based on public health, not industry deals, which would be more straightforward, although probably more difficult politically for Congress to enact since it would not have the industry's blessing.
"Take clear steps to reduce smoking in America without ceding an inch," Kessler advised them, saying he feared the industry was adept at exploiting concessions.
For instance, he said the industry, backing off its Joe Camel and similar ads oriented toward kids, has already introduced ads reeking of sex and glamour aimed at people aged 18-24.

Koop and Kessler were followed by three of the state attorneys general who vigorously defended the tobacco deal they helped to negotiate and said it was a more aggressive anti-tobacco programme than anything Congress or the FDA had achieved in the past 40 years.

They dismissed Koop and Kessler's recommendation as an impossible, unrealistic wish list, but committee chairman Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican, said he was not sure, that the definitions of the possible and the impossible on tobacco were shifting.
"The whole terrain has changed dramatically," said McCain, who added he plans to hold extensive hearings on the proposed industry settlement this fall
In their testimony and to reporters later, Koop and Kessler said that the more they looked at the details of the proposed settlement, the more discouraged they had become.

"During the settlement talks, I was everybody's confidante and adviser, I was on the phone with everybody around that table," Koop told Reuters.. "What I was hearing sounded good, very good, and I kept saying I'd be flexible and wait and see what was in it."
"Then I saw what was in it," he said. "I got to the fine print. It is so underhanded, and unethical."

The two outlined six steps, including giving the FDA clear authority to regulate nicotine, banning cigarette advertising and marketing directed at children, punishing tobacco companies if youth smoking does not decline and banning smoking in all public places.

They also recommended a nationwide programme of public education about tobacco, and programmes to help people who depend on tobacco, whether that means smokers who want to quit or farmers who make their livings from it.
